title: Your HONEY Could Outlive You 🍯
description:
Which outlives you: bread, a banana, or honey? Honey, easily! To germs, honey is a desert: all that sugar slurps the water right out of any germ that lands in it. Keep the lid on, and it can stay good for centuries, way longer than you. And the oldest honey ever found is older than the pyramids. (Maybe don't eat that one.)
Would you taste it? Yes or no?

The science: honey is about 80 % sugar and only about 17 % water, and the sugar holds that water so tightly (a water activity of about 0.6) that there isn't enough free water for most bacteria and moulds. A germ that lands in it loses its own water to the sugar (osmosis) and can't grow. Honey is also acidic (pH about 3.2 to 4.5), and an enzyme the bees add, glucose oxidase, releases a little hydrogen peroxide when honey is diluted. The US National Honey Board says honey in a sealed container can stay stable for decades and even centuries; it may darken or crystallise, which is harmless (warm the jar gently). Keep the lid on: honey that soaks up water can ferment. And babies under 1 should never be given honey: it can carry botulism spores.
The oldest honey yet found: archaeologists in Georgia reported honey traces, identified from their pollen, in clay jars from a tomb about 5,500 years old; the Great Pyramid of Giza is about 4,500 years old. That honey was a residue on the jars' walls, not something you could eat, and the popular story of edible honey from Egyptian tombs has no clear source.
